A release has two steps, and the order is what keeps the site from breaking for anyone mid-visit.

**1. Upload new assets under versioned names.** Every changed file (JS, CSS, images and so on) is uploaded under a name that includes its version, typically a content hash such as `app.3f9a1c.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them has no effect on what users see.

**2. Switch the manifest.** The manifest (or the HTML entry point that plays that role) maps each logical asset to its current versioned filename. Updating it to point at the new names is the moment the release goes live. It's a single small change, so the cutover is effectively atomic.

**Why the upload comes first.** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers start requesting whatever names it lists. If those files aren't already on the server or CDN, the requests fail. Users get missing scripts, unstyled pages or a broken app until the upload finishes. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when the first browser asks for it. This also makes rollback trivial: if something's wrong, point the manifest back at the old names.

**Why we keep the old assets.** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A user who opened the site five minutes before the release still has a page that references the old filenames. When that page lazy-loads a chunk, fetches a font or navigates within the app, it requests old names. If we deleted those files, the user's open session would break with 404s even though nothing is wrong with the new release. Cached copies of the old manifest behave the same way, in browsers and in intermediate caches. Keeping the old assets lets every previously issued manifest keep working until those sessions and caches age out naturally. The versioned names are what make this safe: old and new files never collide, so both releases can be served side by side.

**The rule to remember:** add before you reference, and never remove anything a live manifest might still point to.

Each release uploads every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2e.js`, then switches the manifest so pages reference those names. Assets from the previous release stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment browsers start requesting the new names. If a browser receives the new manifest before an asset has finished uploading, its request for that file returns a 404, and the page loads broken or partly styled. Uploading everything first means that by the time any browser learns a new name, the file is already there. The switch then becomes a single step that takes the whole site from one complete release to the next. Rolling back is the same step in reverse: point the manifest at the previous names.

**Why the old assets stay:** A browser that loaded the page before the switch still holds the old manifest. It keeps requesting the old names as it lazy-loads chunks, follows client-side routes, or fetches images, sometimes hours later in a long-lived tab. CDNs and proxies may also keep serving the cached old manifest for a while after the switch. If we deleted the old files at release time, all of those clients would get 404s in the middle of a session. Because each version has its own names, old and new files never overwrite each other, so keeping the old ones costs only storage. Old assets can be removed once no client could still be using that manifest. Base that point on the manifest's cache lifetime and how long sessions typically run.

Our static-site release has two steps. First, we upload all new assets under versioned names. Then we switch the manifest to point at those names. We don't delete the old assets, so browsers that already fetched the previous manifest can still load them.

The upload comes first because the manifest tells browsers which files to request. As soon as it points to the new names, any browser that fetches it will ask for those files. If we switched first, those requests could hit files that don't exist yet, and the page would fail to load. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when browsers start asking for it.

We keep the old assets because a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names. If we deleted those files, those visitors would get broken pages partway through their session. Versioned names let the old and new files sit side by side, so both groups of browsers get what their manifest promised.
